title: Pippi Longstocking's name came from a child
hook: A sick seven-year-old invented the name Pippi Longstocking out of thin air.
peek: Astrid Lindgren did not invent the name Pippi Longstocking. Her daughter Karin, ill in bed, asked for a story about a girl with that name, made up on the spot. Lindgren told the stories for years before writing them down.
lede: In 1941, Astrid Lindgren's seven-year-old daughter Karin was ill in bed in Stockholm and asked her mother for a story. When Astrid asked what about, Karin said: Pippi Longstocking. She had invented the name right there. Astrid started telling tales about a girl wild enough to match it, and Karin and her friends asked for more for years.

bullets.text: In 1944, while laid up with a sprained ankle, Lindgren wrote the stories down and gave the manuscript to Karin for her tenth birthday. She also sent a copy to a publisher, Bonnier, which turned it down.
Lindgren revised the story and entered it in a children's book competition run by the publisher Rabén & Sjögren. It won first prize, and Pippi Longstocking came out in Sweden in 1945.

In the books, Pippi gives her full name as Pippilotta Delicatessa Windowshade Mackrelmint Efraim's Daughter Longstocking, in one English version. The Swedish surname, Långstrump, simply means long stocking.

Pippi lives alone at Villa Villekulla with a monkey called Mr Nilsson and a horse she can lift over her head. She is the strongest girl in the world, and the stories have been translated into more than 70 languages.
